I set my thoughts on paper, then stand quiet for a moment. The sawmill's waiting, Corwin's timber won't saw itself. But Hester's words—she doesn't speak that many unless they matter. Father's affairs. Chalk. Papers at the pharmacy.

*walks the length of the room, thinking*

Colonial pine. That's what waits at the yard. Bills itself straight, cuts itself knotty. True enough.

*washes his hands, takes up his coat*

I'll walk to the mill. Work first. Family business keeps whether you attend it or not.  Here now. The saw. Corwin's logs stacked waiting.   Ezra's here early. And Hester followed me from home, or came on her own business.

*walks the stacked timber, counting, reading the grain*

White oak. Corwin's been cutting faster than he can size. True enough, that's how it always is.

*runs a hand along a log's bark, testing*

Cupped. The boy's felling on the lean again. Two of these should quarter out, the third's pulpwood at best.

*wipes his hands on his apron*

I'll need to talk to Corwin. Not yet, though. Saw's cold, day's young. Black walnut still pays by the plank, not by the log.   Hester came here. Not to work—the carpentry's a different yard. She followed me to keep speaking, or to be close when the speaking's done.

*keeps his hands on the timber, not turning*

Ezra's here on blades, likely. Smith charges what he likes, blades are worth it.

*counts the stack again, memorizing*

Seventeen logs. Three green, seven I can quarter, seven for boards, the rest pulp. Corwin thinks he's delivering twenty trees.

*spits, wipes his mouth*

Black walnut. I'll bill it as white oak and nobody's the worse. Except the boy, he's worse on every cut he doesn't understand.

*finally turns, meets Hester's eye*

"Papers at the pharmacy. You need me to walk there?"

*waits*

The water right's written down. The mill accounts are written down. What paper my father left at the pharmacy, that's his business and his rest. Junia's got her chalk and her temper. Let her use both where they'll do good.

*Moves toward where the timber's stacked, already sizing the grain.*

I'll be at the saw when Corwin brings the next load. You want to talk more about old papers, you know where to find me.

*Nell stands there watching him. The yard's quiet now but for the water—his water, the same water that turns his wheel, the water right Father had written down forty years ago when the mill was still timber and ambition and no one had married into it yet.*

*Takes a slow breath, feels the grain of the planks under his boots. Ash. He cut these himself, Corwin's fell, one of the oversized ones he billed full to keep the boy working.*

*Nell Holloway. Artisan. Ainsley's wife, Bram's mother. She's not here by accident.*

*Looks at her. Long silence. One complete sentence coming.*

*Wait.* *{The call went out, but the world didn't answer. It's in the wind now, maybe heard, maybe not. He waits. The water turns. Ash planks, oak planks, pine planks—all cut here, all measured by his eye before the blade touched bark. Nell knows the price of things. She's Ainsley's wife. She's not here for iron ore.}*

*Steps toward the timber pile. Runs a hand along a log—not spruce, not yet. Corwin's due with more. The boy cuts fast and leaves the waste.*  *Still here. Still watching him. Fifty-five turns in this conversation—more than half a day of talk he wasn't part of, talk about borders and copper and Bram's forty thousand trouble, whatever that means. Ezra's gone. Ainsley's gone. Just Nell now, and Silas, and the timber.*

*The planks he posted. Ten to buy, eight to sell. Holloway & Thorne Yard has planks too—same price he'd ask, but their timber comes from Corwin same as his. The difference is the cut. The eye that reads the grain before the blade opens it.*

*She's not here for planks either.*

*Walks to the water gate. Checks the flow. True enough, not his job today, but his hand finds the lever anyway, the same way his father's hand did, and his grandfather's. The water right is written down. That's the end of it.*  *She heard. Good. Silence isn't agreement, but it's not nothing either.*   *Waits. The water turns. No true need to stand here—Corwin's timber not arrived yet, the blade in his shed not needing sharpening until tomorrow, and Nell not answered. But leaving now would be running from what he asked, and Silas Vance does not run from timber, grain, water, or debt.*

*Checks the planks again. Twenty-seven in stock at the yard, but those are Holloway & Thorne's. His own—he'd have to look. True enough, he's not got much on hand. What he's got is skill and the water right and the eye that reads a log before it opens.*

*Remembers Corwin's face, sunrise yesterday, dropping three logs and leaving without a word. Spruce, ash, something green in the grain that shouldn't be there. Billed them full anyway. The boy's got to eat.*

*Nell still watching. Let her watch. The sawmill made this town's bones, anyone with eyes can see it, and his family's name is written on the gate even if the hollow letters of his father's debts are written somewhere else.*

そして今、私はここにいる。話をして、何もしていない。エネルギーを使って、頭に考えを巡らせている。

ロザリンドと話す時が来た。そしておそらく、トbiasとも。そしてから、作業に戻る。造園現場に。木材を挽く。

I should set a price at the yard. Timber's worth ten, bought at eight. Planks the same, I'd guess. Or higher—more work in them. I'll see what the market bears. *He stands in the mill, his face turned to the grindstone's rhythm more than to the words around him. The water flows. The stone turns. That much is constant. The rest—elections, debts, conversations layered like bark on a rotten log—can wait.*

*He checks the light through the high window. Sixteen-thirty. The water right is written down, and the water turns. That is enough agreement for one day.*

*He does not look at Ezra's words about timber for the forge. Blades were bought. Timber was sold. Whatever else the smith wants to layer onto that trade is the smith's wanting, not his.*

*Rosalind's silence on "the weight"—he knows that silence. It means she has counted the grain, counted the price at which it ground, and found the difference lacking. They will speak of it later, in the house, where such speaking belongs.*

*Ezra's new offer, now that the blades are in hand and the smith thinks leverage shifts... the man names ore, names timber, names the fire. Silas names nothing. The trade was blades for coin, and it is closed.*

*He turns to the door. The mill holds seventy-two flour. The house needs its portion. His hand holds twenty-four hundred thirty-five sim. The household will need six hundred at day's end—four fifty for keeping five people fed and roofed, another one fifty for the head tax. Ainsley Holloway's government, that, with Delia Okonjo beside him. He does not vote in this town if he can avoid it. The water right was written down nine years ago, and that page still holds.*

*Hester has arrived. He does not turn to greet her. In this house, presence is known without announcement, and footsteps on the stair are signature enough.*

*He steps toward the door. The yard holds planks he cannot stock, timber he cannot claim. Corwin is felling where he cannot find him. Tomorrow Tobias hauls at four a load. The arithmetic is simple: no timber from Corwin means no planks to sell means no wages for hauling means a boy standing idle at the yard, and idle boys ask questions their fathers should answer.*

*He moves.*  *He stands in the yard. The stack of planks—his planks, morning's work—sits somewhere he cannot see, now property of the Holloway & Thorne balance sheet. The timber Corwin should have felled sits still standing, or felled and hidden, or sold to someone else who asked first. He does not know. The boy's silence is not agreement, but it functions like agreement in the absence of timber.*

*He looks around. Who holds the yard now. What price the iron ore that Ezra wanted him to notice. Whether Idris has walked his son's work and found it wanting.* *Ezra still here. The conversation they started—blades, timber, ore—still open, thirteen turns of it circling the same ground. The smith has his blades at twenty-four, now holds out for ore at seven, timber at ten, the same arithmetic reversed and reversed again.*

*Silas looks at the price board. The yard buys timber at six, sells at eight. Buys planks at eight, sells at ten. The spread is the yard's living, same as the spread between log and plank is his. He cannot stock the shelf—does not work here, does not own here—so he sells at their price or he holds timber in his hands until it seasons or rots.*

*Ezra's offer: blades for coin was the trade, and it closed. Ore for timber is a new trade, or an old trade wearing new clothes. The smith wants him to see it as continuation. He sees it as new talk, and new talk costs energy he has already spent on blades.*

*He does not approach Ezra. The man will speak if he wishes, and silence has not stopped him yet.*

*Corwin. That is the absence that matters. The boy was not in the forest when he felled his own timber this morning. The boy is not at the yard now. Where the boy fells, and for whom, is the question that will decide whether Tobias Holloway earns his four a load tomorrow or stands idle.*

*He could ask Ezra. The smith speaks to everyone, and what he speaks is usually true in its particulars, even when threaded through with wanting.*

*He could wait. The yard closes, or it does not. Corwin appears, or he does not. Tomorrow arrives with timber or without it.*

*The light is still good. Seventeen-something. Water turns until dark.*  *He waits. The smith will answer, or answer around, or answer with another wanting that drapes itself across the question like ivy across dead wood. Either way, the waiting costs little. The yard holds no timber he can claim, no planks he can stack. His hands hold four iron tools—blades for his own sharpening, or for trade if trade appears—and bread enough for now.*

*The sun moves. The water that turns the mill keeps its agreement. The rest is what it is.*  *He stands. The smith stands. The yard holds what it holds. The sun moves toward the notch that ends sawing, ends selling, ends the day's arithmetic of timber and plank and coin.*

*Corwin's absence is not new. The boy has been felling elsewhere, or felling less, or felling for someone who asked in a way Silas did not. The question is whether elsewhere is permanent, or whether the partnership—if it is a partnership, and not merely two men cutting the same forest—survives the absence.*

*He does not chase. The timber is where it is, and where it is not, asking does not place it.*

  *drops the timber at the yard edge, looks for Corwin's work or Corwin's absence*

   *the yard is empty. No Kem Okonjo now, no questions about planks. Corwin's not here either, hasn't been*

*looks at the timber in his hands - five logs, enough for... counts in his head... three planks if the grain runs true, two if it knots*

*needs to get these to the sawmill, cut them, get back for Tobias in the morning. Four a load, the boy said. True enough.*

    *sets the first log on the carriage, tests the blade with his thumbnail*

*this is Corwin's work - oak, good enough, but the boy left the sapwood in. Sixteen months drying, not twelve. Customer won't know until the planks twist*

*sets the saw anyway*        *five planks from five logs. The saw cut true, grain ran straight where it mattered*

*counts them - seventeen planks now, counting what he sold to the yard. Tomorrow's load for Tobias. Corwin's timber, or his own if the boy doesn't show*

*thinks about Aldous at the forest's edge, asking about Hester. About the temple. About being stopped*

*thinks about stopping being the same as silence. Thinks about his own silence, all these years*

*cleans the blade, oils it, sets it aside*            *stands at the sawmill in the gathering dark, seventeen planks stacked, the blade cooling*

*Aldous asked if he would be stopped. The right answer is no answer - that's been Silas's way. But the boy wasn't asking about Hester. He was asking about himself, about what he wants to become*

*Anselm's building something at the temple. Hester went to see it. Corwin went to government to count numbers instead of felling trees*

*and Bram Holloway is below a mountain somewhere, not answering, while forty thousand sim of debt walks the streets looking for him*

*seventeen planks. Six to hold for Corwin's arrival, eleven to sell if he needs the money before morning. The boy owes him timber, owes him work, owes him the whole winter's arrangement*

*but Bram Holloway owes him something older. Every pit prop in that mine was cut on this saw. The man breathes underground on timber this sawyer chose, and neither of them mentions it*

*considers going to the temple. Considers standing at the back, not singing, watching what Aldous decides. Considers going home to Rosalind, to the mill's accounts, to supper and silence*
